data.text/html:
Sir, this is a classification task

An interactive companion to marimo's video "Sir, This is a Classification Task", about GLiNER-style encoder models.
Everyone is fine-tuning LLMs like Qwen into decision models (classifiers). It works. But a model built to generate text may be an expensive way to pick one of three labels. Do we need the decoder at all?
The video's answer, rebuilt here with things you can click: cost of the two architectures → contextualised embeddings → labels as input tokens → entities as spans → label descriptions → sandbox & quiz.

data.text/markdown:
1. Two ways to build a decision model

The popular way (fine-tuned decoder). Take a Qwen model, fine-tune it so that after reading the prompt it samples a token that happens to be a class name. The whole generative stack is still there: the transformer blocks, a language-model head that scores every word in a ~150k vocabulary, and a sampling loop that runs once per generated token. The video's question. The transformer blocks alone already produce contextualised embeddings, one per input token. If we could read a decision straight off those embeddings, we could drop the decoding machinery and, in the GLiNER family, use a much smaller encoder (BERT/DeBERTa-sized, a few hundred million parameters) that runs on a CPU.

data.text/markdown:
How much compute does each design use?

A useful rule of thumb: a transformer forward pass costs about ||[\text{FLOPs} \approx 2 \cdot N_\text{params} \cdot N_\text{tokens}.||]The decoder reads the prompt (instructions, the label list and the text) and then runs one more pass per generated token. The encoder reads text and label tokens once. These are rough assumptions for an order-of-magnitude comparison, not benchmarks. Accuracy is not part of this calculation. The video's own benchmark found the fine-tuned GLiNER-style models competitive, with the caveat that the dataset may have leaked into pre-training.

The toy encoder used in the rest of this notebook

The next three cells are the whole model. Read them: there is nothing hidden.
  • embed(token): a lookup in the hand-made table below. Special tokens and stop words are zero vectors. Unknown words get a deterministic random direction, so the toy "doesn't know" them. Capitalised unknown words lean towards person/place, a crude stand-in for what a real model learns about names.
  • encode(...): two layers of ||(H \leftarrow \operatorname{unit}\big(H + \operatorname{softmax}(HH^\top / T)\,H\big)||), attention with query = key = value = ||(H||). Label blocks may attend to themselves and to the text. The text attends only to itself (GLiNER uses full attention; we isolate the labels so each one is an independent decision).
  • the head: ||(\text{logit} = 12\,(\cos(\text{label}, \text{text}) - 0.75)||) followed by a sigmoid (independent labels) or a softmax (mutually exclusive labels). In a real model this head is learned. Here it is fixed.

2. Contextualised embeddings: every token looks at every other token

The video's mental model of attention: each token's embedding is compared with all the other embeddings, and the token's new embedding is a weighted mix of the tokens it found similar. After a few layers, every output "knows" about its context. Here is the video's input sequence with the labels written into the sequence: [BOS] [LABEL] refund [LABEL] outage [LABEL] praise [SEP] my card got charged twice Click a token in the explorer (hover previews it). Arcs show where that token's attention goes in the chosen layer: thicker arc = more weight. With the default settings, the green refund token sends most of its attention to card and charged, while the purple praise finds nothing in the text it resembles.

data.text/markdown:
3. The trick: labels are just more input tokens

Once the labels sit in the input sequence, each label gets its own contextualised output embedding. A small classification head compares it with the text and returns one score per label: ||[\text{logit}_\ell = 12\,\big(\cos(\mathbf h_\ell, \bar{\mathbf h}_\text{text}) - 0.75\big)||]
  • independent labels → ||(p_\ell = \sigma(\text{logit}_\ell)||). Each label is its own yes/no question, so several can be "on" (multi-label).
  • mutually exclusive labels → ||(p = \operatorname{softmax}(\text{logit})||). Exactly one class wins, like a scikit-learn classifier.
Because the label is input rather than a fixed output neuron, you can rename or add a label without retraining (the video's shipping example), and you can ask several questions at once, e.g. a topic and a mood.

data.text/html: Top topic: refund (p = 0.95). The sequence has 17 tokens, of which 10 are label tokens: that is the context cost of the trick.

The new label wins, though no model weights changed.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSigmoid vs softmax:\u003c/strong\u003e with the text \u003cem\u003e\"thanks, the app crashed again\"\u003c/em\u003e and labels \u003ccode\u003epraise, outage, refund\u003c/code\u003e, sigmoid gives outage ≈ 0.9 and still leaves praise ≈ 0.3\n   (each label is judged on its own). Softmax makes them compete, so praise drops to ≈ 0.04. Which one fits your problem?\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eZero-shot limits:\u003c/strong\u003e add the label \u003ccode\u003echargeback\u003c/code\u003e. The toy has never seen this word, so its embedding is random and it scores ≈ 0.\n   Section 5 fixes this with a \u003cem\u003edescription\u003c/em\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNotice that the \u003cstrong\u003emood head\u003c/strong\u003e runs on the same text in the same forward pass. It is a second, independent decision.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"neutral"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4. Per entity: from labels to spans (named entity recognition)

Same encoder, new sentence: "Ada Lovelace visited New York in May." Now we don't want one label for the whole text. We want to find which pieces of the text are a person, a location or a date. The special token changes from [LABEL] to [ENT]: [BOS] [ENT] person [ENT] location [ENT] date [SEP] Ada Lovelace visited New York in May Then, GLiNER-style:
  1. Enumerate spans: every run of 1 … max width consecutive tokens (Ada, Ada Lovelace, Lovelace visited, …).
  2. Embed each span by aggregating its tokens' contextualised outputs (mean, first+last, or max).
  3. Score every (span, entity type) pair with the same head: ||(\sigma\big(12(\cos(\mathbf h_\text{span}, \mathbf h_\text{ent}) + \beta\,(w-1) - 0.75)\big)||), where ||(\beta||) is a small toy length bonus. A trained model learns such preferences.
  4. Decode greedily: keep the highest-scoring span above the threshold, discard spans that overlap it, and repeat.
(Toy rule: spans may not start or end on a stop word such as in. Real models learn this as well.)
14 candidate spans × 3 entity types = 42 scores → 3 entities kept: Ada Lovelace → person, New York → location, May → date

data.text/markdown:
5. Another trick: give each label a description

One word can be a thin description of a class. So, as in the video, append a description after each label behind a new special token: [BOS] [LABEL] refund [DESC] wants money back [LABEL] outage [DESC] service is down … [SEP] my card got charged twice The label's final embedding is now shaped by its description and by the text. You hope its attention goes to the description of its own label plus the relevant text tokens. A real model may need fine-tuning to learn that. In our toy, the label representation is the mean of the outputs of the name and description tokens.

data.text/markdown:
6. Sandbox: your own decision model

Write any text, any labels and any entity types. One "encoder pass" per head, no retraining, no decoder. The toy only knows its small vocabulary (open the toy_vocab cell to see it, or add words there).

Quiz: predict, then reveal

Commit to your answers before you flip the reveal switch. The answers come from the same toy model, so you can reason from the embedding table (section 1) and the attention explorer (section 2).
Answer all five, then flip reveal answers.

Recap

Fine-tuned decoder LLM (e.g. Qwen 0.8B-4B) Encoder + label tokens (GLiNER-style)
How a decision is made generate the class name token by token score each label's contextual embedding against the text
Parts of the network used all of it: blocks, LM head over the full vocabulary, sampling loop encoder blocks + a small head
Typical size billions of parameters ~0.1–0.5B parameters (roughly an order of magnitude less)
CPU-friendly painful often yes
Change or add a label edit the prompt; output may drift; usually re-tune just change the label token, no retraining needed (zero-shot)
Several decisions at once longer prompt, structured output extra label blocks or independent heads, still one pass
Entities / spans ask the model to list substrings score every span against [ENT] tokens
Richer label meaning longer instructions [DESC] description tokens
Cost of the trick prompt tokens label tokens eat a little context
Guarantees on the output it may produce a non-label string the output is always a score for each label you provided
Main takeaways from the video: if the job is classification, you may not need the parts of a generative model that generate. The encoder's contextualised embeddings already hold the information. Labels (and entity types, and descriptions) can be fed in as input tokens, which keeps the model flexible. Extensions (real models). Install the gliner package (pip install gliner) and load a pretrained GLiNER checkpoint. model.predict_entities(text, ["person", "location", "date"], threshold=0.5) does section 4 with learned weights. Fastino hosts the GLiNER family, GLiNER2 (classification + entities + structure in one encoder) and their "Glide" decision model. See the links under the video. Compare its predictions on the sandbox sentences with this toy. A good exercise: re-implement score_spans with real token embeddings from a small BERT.
